newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn gold feud pits Bundestag against Bundesbank.
newsitem.headline: Bonn gold feud pits Bundestag against Bundesbank.

text.p: Germany's unprecedented gold battle turned into a clash of institutions on Saturday as key allies of Chancellor Helmut Kohl told the powerful Bundesbank to respect the independece of the Bonn parliament, the Bundestag.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, whose plan to revalue gold and currency reserves to qualify for Europe's monetary union (EMU) angered the central bank, drew a clear line between the bank's monetary policy power and Bonn's law-making role.
Wolfgang Schaeuble, the parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats, made the same confrontational point in a letter to deputies urging them to back Waigel's plan.

The comments came after Der Spiegel magazine quoted Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer as asking whether Bonn and Paris could delay the 1999 start of the single currency rather than revalue the reserves in a way many Germans see as an unacceptable case of "creative accounting."

"I expect the Bundesbank to respect the legislative independence of politics just as politics always respects the independence of the Bundesbank in monetary policy," Waigel told journalists in Pfaffenhausen, a southern German resort, during a bicycle tour on this holiday weekend.

The comments by Waigel and Schaeuble, the latest escalation in Germany's bullion battle, aimed at turning the red-hot issue into a question of institutional powers rather than a showdown between Kohl and Tietmeyer, a former protege of the chancellor.
The Bundesbank is by far Germany's most trusted institution and commentators say taking it on for an unpopular goal -- Europe's single currency -- could be a huge political blunder.
Waigel, who has rejected loud opposition calls for his resignation was at pains to defuse the personal angle.
"I have no problems with Hans Tietmeyer," he declared.
Waigel also said he saw no opposition among CDU deputies to the gold plan, which parliament will begin debating on Thursday.

At least two coalition deputies -- one CDU and one from the allied Free Democratic Party (FDP) -- have come out against the plan. Kohl commands only five votes more than the absolute majority he needs to change the Bundesbank law in parliament.
In his letter, Schaeuble told his faction that parliament's independence was just as important as the much-vaunted autonomy of the central bank.

Schaeuble, Kohl's chief lieutenant, also said Germany must do everything possible to fulfil its legal obligation to meet the criteria and timetable for a single European currency. The revaluation plan helped reach these targets, he said.

"The decision on the question we now face is to be taken by the legislature, whose independence is not less than that of the Bundesbank," Schaeuble wrote, according to extracts of the letter released by the Welt am Sonntag weekly on Saturday.
News of the letter, expected to be in deputies' mail boxes on Monday morning, emerged as opposition to the plan appeared to be growing among Kohl's centre-right coalition.

"The finance minister wanted to fool us into believing that there would be no problems with the Bundesbank over the revaluation of the gold and currency supplies," FDP budget policy expert Juergen Koppelin told the Bild daily.
"Waigel should now give up his plan. The psychological damage would be too great."

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said Kohl should call a general election as his coalition was now so split over how to fill projected shortfalls in government finances for 1997 and 1998 and meet the membership criteria for the single currency.

"The economic and finance policies of the Kohl government have failed. The coalition is so split it's not capable of acting. It would be good for Germany if it cleared the path for fresh elections," SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said.
"The international reaction to the government's gold plans has been catastrophic," Lafontaine said in an interview with the news magazine Der Spiegel to be published in Monday's edition.
Waigel wants to use the windfall from revaluing the gold and currency reserves to retire debt. Schaeuble said this was the correct solution to Germany's budget problems.

"The legislative decision necessary is in no way interference in the legally defined independence of the Bundesbank and it does not endanger the stability of the deutschemark," he wrote in his letter.
